evidence.quote: Peter Drucker was one of the most important management thinkers of the past hundred years. He wrote about 40 books and thousands of articles and he never rested in his mission to persuade the world that management matters. Management is the organ of institutions—the organ that converts a mob into an organisation, and human efforts into performance. Did he succeed? The range of his influence was extraordinary. Wherever people grapple with tricky management problems in big organisations and small ones the world over, in the public sector and the private, and increasingly in the voluntary sector, you can find Drucker's fingerprints.

14.explanation: Drucker có ảnh hưởng rộng ở nhiều loại tổ chức.

evidence.quote: His first two books, The End of Economic Man (1939) and The Future of Industrial Man (1942), had their admirers, but they annoyed academic critics by ranging so widely over so many different subjects. Still, the second of these books attracted attention with its insistence that companies had a social dimension as well as an economic purpose. His third book, The Concept of the Corporation, became an instant bestseller in the 1940s and has remained in print ever since.

15.explanation: Đoạn B trình bày ba cuốn sách đầu tiên.

evidence.quote: The two most interesting arguments in The Concept of the Corporation dominated his later work. The first had to do with empowering workers. Drucker believed in treating workers as resources rather than just as costs. He was a harsh critic of the assembly-line system of production, partly because assembly lines moved at the speed of the slowest and partly because they failed to engage the creativity of individual workers. The second argument had to do with the rise of knowledge workers. Drucker argued that the world was moving from an 'economy of goods' to an 'economy of knowledge', which he insisted had profound implications for both managers and politicians. Managers had to stop treating workers like cogs in a huge inhuman machine and start treating them as brain workers. Politicians had to realise that knowledge, and hence education, was the single most important resource for any advanced society. Yet Drucker also thought this economy had implications for knowledge workers themselves. They had to come to terms with the fact that they were not simply bosses or 'workers' but something in between—entrepreneurs who had responsibility for developing their most important resource, brainpower, and who also needed to take more control of their own careers.

16.explanation: Nhân viên chuyển từ lao động như bánh răng sang lao động tri thức.

evidence.quote: However, there was also a hard side to his work. Drucker was responsible for inventing one of the rational school of management's most successful products—'management by objectives'. In one of his most substantial works, The Practice of Management (1954), he emphasised the importance of managers and corporations setting clear long-term objectives and then translating these into more immediate goals. For his critics, this was a retreat from his earlier emphasis on the soft side of management. For Drucker, it was all consistent—if you rely too much on empowerment you risk anarchy, whereas if you rely too much on command and control you sacrifice creativity. The trick is for managers to set long-term goals but then allow their workers to find ways of achieving those goals. If Drucker helped make management a global industry, he also helped push it beyond its business base. He was emphatically a management thinker, not just a business one. He believed that management is 'the defining organ of all modern institutions', not just of business corporations.

17.explanation: Quản lý cần cân bằng mục tiêu rõ ràng với tự do thực hiện.

evidence.quote: There have been three persistent criticisms of Drucker's work. The first is that he focused on big organisations rather than small ones. The Concept of the Corporation was in many ways a tribute to big organisations. As Drucker said, 'We know today that in modern industrial production, particularly in modern mass production, the small unit is not only inefficient, it cannot produce at all'. The book helped to launch the 'big organisation boom' that dominated business thinking for the next 20 years. The second criticism is that Drucker's enthusiasm for management by objectives helped to lead business down a dead end. Most of today's best organisations have abandoned this idea. They prefer to allow ideas to bubble up from the bottom and middle of the organisations rather than being imposed from on high. Thirdly, Drucker is criticised for lacking real commitment and precise knowledge. He never mastered the rigours of his chosen field and there is no single area of management he made his own.

18.explanation: Đoạn E tổng hợp ba phê bình.

evidence.quote: There is some truth in the first two arguments. Drucker never wrote anything as good on small businesses as The Concept of the Corporation. His work on management by objectives sits uneasily with his earlier and later writing on the importance of knowledge workers and self-directed teams. But the third argument is short-sighted because it ignores Drucker's pioneering role in creating the modern profession of management. He produced one of the first systematic studies of a big company and was the first to stress that ideas can help galvanise companies. The biggest problem with evaluating Drucker's influence is that so many of his ideas have passed into conventional wisdom—in other words, he is a victim of his own success. His ideas on the importance of knowledge workers and empowerment may seem obvious today, but they certainly weren't when he conceived them in the 1940s, or when they were put into practice in the 1980s.

evidence.quote: The major challenge of the gallery renovation project was that it involved two parts. evidence.quote: A 2003 survey of young people's impressions of the gallery confirmed this opinion, sounding more like references to an abandoned building. For those young people Auckland Art Gallery was undemocratic, 'dusty' and 'cold' - the epitome of threshold fear. Also, 16% of the sample group had no idea where it even was, despite being interviewed on the pavement right outside it. Clearly, the gallery was fatally out of step at a time when New Zealand's national museum in Wellington was successfully engaging broader audiences with contemporary branding and marketing, interactive displays and temporary events.

evidence.quote: Recently, social scientists have begun to identify the consequences of living at increasingly smaller distances from other people. However, before we consider this research, it is important for us to understand the difference between two terms: density and crowding. Density is a measure of the space available to people in a given area. Crowding, on the other hand, is a psychological state rather than a physical measure. You can feel crowded, but you cannot 'feel' density. Density and crowding are often related but, as we will see later, this is not always the case.

1.explanation: Đoạn B phân biệt mật độ vật lý với cảm giác chen chúc.

evidence.quote: In 1962, a researcher named John Calhoun published the results of a study that shocked social scientists and added a new urgency to the study of density and crowding. Calhoun built a rat colony with four rooms designed to hold about 48 animals. However, he let the population grow until it reached 80. The rats were given enough food, water and nesting material to maintain a high standard of living, but problems soon began to develop. Some dominant rats laid claim to two of the rooms, forcing the rest of the rats to live in the remaining two rooms. As a result of overcrowding. these two areas became behavioural sinks, which aggravated all forms of normally unacceptable social behaviour.

2.explanation: Đoạn C mô tả thí nghiệm chuột và kết quả.

evidence.quote: In response to Calhoun's experiment with the rat colony, a number of investigators then conducted studies comparing the behaviour of human individuals living in different densities. The results of these studies were interesting: some found bad effects (high rates of mental illness and juvenile delinquency) associated with high density, while others did not. Furthermore, even in the studies that reported negative behaviour related to high density, it was not possible to know for sure that high density was the cause of the problem. For example, the highest density areas are usually found in the inner cities, and residents of these are often poorer, less educated and have less job security than people living in the lower density suburbs.

3.explanation: Nghiên cứu ở người nối tiếp thí nghiệm Calhoun.

evidence.quote: After an examination of the effects of density, researchers began to turn their attention to identifying the conditions under which high density leads to crowding, stress and behavioural effects. A number of factors have been found to influence the amount of crowding people will experience. First, the focus of our attention determines when we will feel crowded. When other people who are violating our personal space become the centre of our attention, we will attribute our arousal and discomfort to their closeness. This will result in our feeling crowded. For example, at an athletics event people's attention is focused on the competition and not on the other spectators: as a result, they are not likely to experience much crowding. But if the spectators are trying to leave the area after the event is over, they may experience crowding because they now see other people as preventing them from leaving as quickly as they would like to. Another area where high density may lead to crowding is when people feel that they have no control over their environment. The experience of a person in a packed department store can lead to feelings of utter helplessness; not only is it difficult to get to the cashier, but it is not possible to go against the flow of people moving into the store. Crowding is also likely to be felt when people cannot achieve the kind of privacy they want. Privacy means being able to choose whether or not to interact with others. When high density forces us to interact with others against our will, we may experience crowding.

4.explanation: Đoạn E nêu điều kiện tạo cảm giác chen chúc.

evidence.quote: While high density by itself does not necessarily lead to negative reactions from people, the research on crowding presents a different picture. Crowding often has a negative impact on our emotions, performance and interpersonal relations. One common result is that we are less attracted to people in crowded than in non-crowded conditions. Interestingly enough, this effect has been consistently found for males but not for females. This may be due to the larger personal space areas (zones) that males have or else to a tendency for females to act co-operatively, while males are more likely to respond to others competitively. This may explain why there is often a high incidence of violence in male prisons. Also, in addition to tending toward aggression, people are less likely to help others in crowded, as opposed to non-crowded, environments.

5.explanation: Chen chúc tác động tới cảm xúc, quan hệ và hành vi.

evidence.quote: The distinction between density and crowding also has some important implications for managing our environment. The first implication is that giving people more space will not necessarily reduce their sense of crowding. Secondly, crowding can be reduced without reducing density. For example, it was found that people who felt that they could easily leave a room full of people felt less crowded than people who thought it would be difficult to leave. Other research supporting this has found that people feel less crowded in high density environments if they have control. In another study, it was found that people felt less crowded and performed better in a room with pictures on the walls than in a room with no pictures, even though the density was the same in both situations. The investigators argued that the pictures made the presence of other people less obvious and thereby reduced crowding. Thus, there are many ways that crowding and its effects can be reduced without increasing space or decreasing the number of people in the environment.

6.explanation: Phân biệt mật độ và cảm giác chen chúc gợi cách quản lý môi trường.

evidence.quote: After an examination of the effects of density, researchers began to turn their attention to identifying the conditions under which high density leads to crowding, stress and behavioural effects. A number of factors have been found to influence the amount of crowding people will experience. First, the focus of our attention determines when we will feel crowded. When other people who are violating our personal space become the centre of our attention, we will attribute our arousal and discomfort to their closeness. This will result in our feeling crowded. For example, at an athletics event people's attention is focused on the competition and not on the other spectators: as a result, they are not likely to experience much crowding. But if the spectators are trying to leave the area after the event is over, they may experience crowding because they now see other people as preventing them from leaving as quickly as they would like to. Another area where high density may lead to crowding is when people feel that they have no control over their environment. The experience of a person in a packed department store can lead to feelings of utter helplessness; not only is it difficult to get to the cashier, but it is not possible to go against the flow of people moving into the store. Crowding is also likely to be felt when people cannot achieve the kind of privacy they want. Privacy means being able to choose whether or not to interact with others. When high density forces us to interact with others against our will, we may experience crowding.

evidence.quote: Not all chocolate is created equal, however. Dark chocolate gets all the good publicity because it has relatively lower added sugar and fats than milk chocolate. The benefits come from cocoa,’ Pereira notes — thus, ‘chocolates with the highest proportion of cocoa are better.’ Even when it comes to pure cocoa, which can be used for a hot beverage or added as a topping, he acknowledges that no one knows the ideal amount. Even the darkest of the dark chocolates ‘must be consumed in moderation to avoid weight gain’, he notes. Finley and his team went straight for the pure, unsweetened cocoa to test its impact on gut microbes. Nevertheless, each type produced slightly different results. The researchers sent three types of cocoa down the lab-rigged digestive path: lightly processed, moderately processed and Dutch-processed. The more mildly treated the cocoa, the more it produced beneficial compounds in these experiments. Farhat also noted that likewise some brands of dark chocolate ‘are low in antioxidants due to the methods of manufacturing’.

14.explanation: Thử ba loại cacao có mức xử lý khác nhau.

evidence.quote: Previous research suggested that cocoa components could be fermented, or chemically changed, to generate beneficial compounds. Daily consumption of dark chocolate or cocoa lowered people’s blood pressure, according to a 2012 review of 20 different studies. John Finley, a professor of food sciences at Louisiana State University in the US, and his students took the work a step further to see what else the body might be getting from this common treat - and how. To follow cocoa through its digestive journey, they created a lab-built gut, and discovered that microbes feasted on what was left of the cocoa after its passage through the simulated digestive system. They fermented these compounds, called flavonols, into smaller anti-inflammatory chemicals that could be absorbed into the bloodstream.

15.explanation: Vi khuẩn lên men flavonol thành chất chống viêm hấp thu được.

evidence.quote: Of course, ‘chocolate is not a substitute for prescribed medications’, Pereira notes. He suggests cocoa might work best for people who fall in the middle of the bell curve for cardiovascular health. If you have a patient with severely impaired vascular function, you cannot expect benefits from chocolate,’ he says. And likewise, those who are already exceedingly healthy might not see much of a boost from extra cocoa. But both he and Finley suggest that cocoa could help in the effort to prevent heart disease. ‘Dark chocolate could well be a preventative nutritional supplement to consider,’ Pereira says. ‘Or a preventative snack.’

16.explanation: Người mạch máu quá yếu hoặc đã rất khỏe có thể ít hưởng lợi.

evidence.quote: With the high levels of antioxidants, cocoa might also be good for the gut itself. It appears that if you were consuming some cocoas, it would actually stimulate the production of healthier microbes in the colon,’ Finley says. Additionally, the microbes broke down the undigested fiber in the cocoa. The bottom line is that now I put cocoa on my oatmeal,’ Finley says. Although his wife dismisses the non-traditional topping as a bit weird, Finley has science on his side for his breakfast combo: The anti-inflammatory compounds combined with dietary fiber is a synergistic effect - one and one makes three’ in this case, he says. And combining cocoa with additional sources of dietary fiber might boost the effect even more. As Finley suggests, ‘maybe chocolate-covered black beans?’

17.explanation: Finley rắc cacao lên oatmeal, cách dùng vợ ông thấy lạ.

evidence.quote: This simulated bodily process seems plausible from both a biological and chemical standpoint, says Telmo Pereira of the Department of Cardiopneumology at the Superior College of Health Technology in Portugal. The next step, of course, will be more testing and looking for this transformation in humans, he notes. As Grace Farhat, a researcher in the Department of Dietetics, Nutrition and Biological Sciences at Queen Margaret University in Edinburgh, points out, we can’t be entirely sure that each person’s gut will undertake the same fermentation processes. The composition of bacteria will vary in different individuals,’ she says. This will mean certain individuals may derive more benefits than others.’

evidence.quote: These new findings, however, could help explain why dark chocolate improves vascular function and cardiovascular health in general. Other recent research has found that regular, moderate consumption of dark chocolate offers benefits even for the young and healthy. Pereira and colleagues found that healthy young adults who ate eight grams — about one small square — of 70 percent cocoa chocolate each day for a month had ‘an obvious improvement’ in vascular function compared to a control group. Those eating the extra chocolate saw their blood flow increasing, on average, from 14 percent to 23 percent. The findings were published earlier this year and could have substantial implications for health on a broader population scale. ‘Tf consuming dark chocolate in moderate quantities has the ability to decrease the risk of heart disease, it could have a role to play in reducing medical costs as well,’ Farhat says.

evidence.quote: Though the revival of a mammoth is no longer mere fantasy, the reality is still years away. For another extinct species, the time frame may be shorter. A group of scientists led by Michael Archer are hoping to revive a type of Australian frog. Archer previously directed a highly publicized attempt to clone the thylacine, a marsupial carnivore that went extinct in the 1930s, but this failed. Wary of the expectations that such high-profile experiments attract, Archer kept quiet about his team's new efforts until they had some preliminary results to offer; in fact they have now produced a number of embryos.

14.explanation: Thất bại dự án thylacine khiến Archer thận trọng với kỳ vọng công chúng.

evidence.quote: In the popular imagination, people think of dinosaurs being brought back to life. In reality the only species we can hope to revive are those that died within the past few tens of thousands of years and left behind remains containing intact cells, or enough ancient DNA to reconstruct the creature's genome. Because of the natural rates of decay, retrieving the full genome of dinosaurs is not feasible. The species theoretically capable of being revived all disappeared while humanity was climbing toward world domination. ‘If we're talking about species that we drove extinct, then I think we have an obligation to try to do this,’ says Michael Archer, a palaeontologist at the University of New South Wales in Australia.

15.explanation: Phải còn tế bào hay đủ DNA nên không hồi sinh khủng long được.

evidence.quote: Other scientists who favour de-extinction argue that there will be concrete benefits. Most pharmaceutical drugs, for example, have been derived from natural compounds found in wild flowers and shrubs, some of which are now also vulnerable to extinction. Some extinct animals performed vital services within their ecosystems, which might do well from their return. Siberia, for example, was once home to mammoths and other grazing mammals. Then, the landscape was not moss-dominated tundra but grassy steppes. Russian ecologist Sergey Zimov argues that this was no coincidence: the mammoths and numerous herbivores maintained the grassland by breaking up the soil and fertilizing it with their manure. Once they were gone, moss took over and transformed the grassland into less productive tundra.

16.explanation: Thực vật tự nhiên là nguồn hợp chất dược phẩm.

evidence.quote: When Fernández-Arias first tried to bring back the bucardo ten years ago, the cloning tools at his disposal were very basic, but over the past decade scientists have improved their success in cloning non-extinct animals with the help of advanced scientific techniques. Korean and Russian researchers now aim to clone a mammoth, and have found pieces of mammoth tissue in Siberian ice. They need a cell that's still alive, but most scientists doubt that one could have survived the freezing temperatures. However, Insung Hwang, the Korean team leader, says ‘If you don't try, how would you know that it's impossible?’

17.explanation: Kỹ thuật nhân bản hiện nay tiến bộ hơn mười năm trước.

evidence.quote: For thousands of years a wild goat known as a bucardo endured harsh winters in the range of mountains that divides France from Spain, surviving on leaves and stems. As humans began to settle, hunting drove down the bucardo population over several centuries. By 1999 a single bucardo remained – a female nicknamed Celia. A team led by wildlife veterinarian Alberto Fernández-Arias clipped a tiny radio around her neck, and released her into the wild. Nine months later came a long beep: this told them that Celia had died. The bucardo became officially extinct. But Celia's cells lived on, preserved in laboratories. Over the next few years, a team of reproductive physiologists led by José Folch injected nuclei from those cells into goat eggs, then implanted the eggs in surrogate mothers. After 57 implantations, only seven animals had become pregnant, and of those seven pregnancies, only one continued to full term. And then, as Fernández-Arias held the newborn bucardo, he could see that she was struggling and despite efforts to help her breathe, the clone died. So far, Celia's clone is the closest anyone has gotten to bringing an extinct species back to life. Since then, remarkable advances have been made in manipulating stem cells, and in reconstructing lost genomes, the complete set of genetic material of an organism. It seems that de-extinction is within reach.

Most pharmaceutical drugs, for example, have been derived from natural compounds found in wild flowers and shrubs, some of which are now also vulnerable to extinction. Some extinct animals performed vital services within their ecosystems, which might do well from their return. Siberia, for example, was once home to mammoths and other grazing mammals. Then, the landscape was not moss-dominated tundra but grassy steppes. Russian ecologist Sergey Zimov argues that this was no coincidence: the mammoths and numerous herbivores maintained the grassland by breaking up the soil and fertilizing it with their manure. Once they were gone, moss took over and transformed the grassland into less productive tundra.

24.explanation: Zimov liên hệ động vật ăn cỏ với duy trì đồng cỏ.

evidence.quote: But just because we potentially can bring back extinct species, does this mean we should? ‘There is clearly a terrible urgency to saving threatened species,’ says John Wiens, an evolutionary biologist at Stony Brook University in New York. ‘As far as I can see, there is little urgency for bringing back extinct ones. Why invest dollars in bringing a handful of species back from the dead, when there are millions still waiting to be protected?’ There is also the issue of whether a clone is truly an example of its species, or just an engineered curiosity. And would it need to be introduced into the wild to be truly de-extinct?

25.explanation: Wiens ưu tiên bảo vệ loài còn sống bị đe dọa.

evidence.quote: Conservation biologist Stuart Pimm points to the huge effort that went into restoring the Arabian oryx to the wild. After the animals were placed in a refuge, almost all were killed by hunters, making the project a failure. ‘We had the animals, and we put them back, and the world wasn’t ready,’ says Pimm. ‘Having the species solves only a tiny part of the problem.’ Even if de-extinction proved a logistical success, what impact would the introduction of a genetically engineered organism into the environment have? Could a revived species spread a virus that might wipe out other species? De-extinction advocates are pondering these questions and most believe they need to be resolved before any project moves forward.

26.explanation: Pimm cảnh báo đưa động vật lại nơi vẫn bị săn sẽ thất bại.

evidence.quote: To establish cause and effect, researchers at Baumeister’s lab tried refuelling the brain in experiments involving lemonade mixed either with sugar or with a diet sweetener. The sugary lemonade provided a burst of glucose, the effects of which could be observed immediately in the lab; the sugarless sweeteners tasted similar but did not contain the glucose. Again and again, the sugar restored willpower, but the artificial sweetener had no effect. The glucose would mitigate the ego depletion and sometimes completely reverse it, improving self-control and the quality of decisions: the subjects resisted national bias when making choices and, when making financial decisions, they were more likely to choose the better long-term strategy instead of going for a quick payoff.

14.explanation: Lemonade có đường và chất ngọt nhân tạo có vị giống nhưng tác động khác.

evidence.quote: Decision fatigue involves a phenomenon called ego depletion, a term coined by social psychologist Roy F. Baumeister. His research demonstrated that there is a finite store of mental stamina for exerting self-control. For example, when people fended off the temptation to eat freshly baked biscuits, they were then less able to resist other temptations. When they tried to resist the urge to cry during a sad movie, afterwards they gave up more quickly on tasks requiring self-discipline, such as working on a geometry puzzle. The experiments confirmed the 19th-century notion of willpower being like a muscle that became tired with use; something which could be conserved by avoiding temptation.

15.explanation: Kìm khóc khi xem phim buồn làm người ta bỏ nhiệm vụ sớm hơn.

evidence.quote: ‘Good decision-making is not a trait of the person,’ Baumeister says. ‘It's a slate that fluctuates.’ His studies show that people with the best self-control are the ones who avoid temptations, and who establish habits that eliminate the mental effort of making choices. Instead of counting on willpower all day, they conserve it so that it's available for important decisions. ‘Even the wisest people won't make good choices when they're not rested and their glucose is low,’ Baumeister notes. If a decision must be made late in the afternoon or in the evening, they know not to do it on an empty stomach. The best decision-makers, according to Baumeister, ‘are the ones who know when not to trust themselves.’

16.explanation: Đói và glucose thấp khiến quyết định cuối ngày kém.

evidence.quote: However, some brain researchers had reservations about the glucose connection. Todd Heatherton, a pioneer of social neuroscience, believed in ego depletion but didn't see how this process could be caused simply by variations in glucose levels. To observe the process, and to see if it could be reversed by glucose, Heatherton's team recorded images of the brains of 45 people who were on a low calorie diet as they reacted to pictures of food. Next, these dieters watched a comedy video while forcing themselves to suppress their laughter - thereby draining mental energy and inducing ego depletion. When they were again shown pictures of food, further brain scans revealed more activity in the brain's reward centre and a decrease in the amygdale, which helps control impulses. The food's appeal, in other words, registered more strongly white impulse control weakened. What surprised Heatherton was that administering glucose completely reversed the brain changes brought about by ego depletion.

17.explanation: Heatherton ban đầu nghi ngờ mối liên hệ đơn giản với glucose.

evidence.quote: Decision fatigue leaves people vulnerable to marketers who know how to time their sales, as Jonathan Levav demonstrated. He visited a tailor to have a suit made for his wedding and began going through the choices of fabric, buttons and so forth and when he got through the third pile of fabric samples. Levav recalls, ‘I couldn’t tell the choices apart anymore. After a while my only response to the tailor became, ‘What do you recommend?’ Levav put the experience to use in an experiment conducted at German car dealerships, where real customers had to choose among four styles of gearshift knobs, 25 configurations of the engine and gearbox and a palette of 56 colours for the interior. As they started picking features, customers would carefully weigh the choices, but as decision fatigue set in they would start settling for the default option. By manipulating the order of the car buyers’ choices, the researchers found that customers would end up paying more.

18.explanation: Kinh nghiệm chọn đồ may cưới dẫn Levav đến thí nghiệm mua xe.

evidence.quote: Similarly, sweet snacks are featured prominently at cash registers at most supermarkets. With their willpower reduced after shopping, people are especially vulnerable to sweet drinks and snacks. While supermarkets figured this out a long time ago, only recently did researchers discover why. Baumeister’s research team tested the notion that people fight off temptation best by indulging in just a little of it, finding that a delicious, thick milkshake strengthened willpower by helping people perform better than expected on their next task. However, the experiment also included a control group who drank a tasteless low-fat dairy beverage. It provided them with no pleasure, yet it produced similar improvements in self-control. Baumeister concluded that even the tasteless drink had worked because the brain, like the rest of the body, derived energy from glucose, the simple sugar manufactured from a kind of foods including milk.

19.explanation: Đồ ngọt ở quầy thanh toán tận dụng ý chí đã giảm sau mua sắm.

evidence.quote: No matter how rational people try to be, they can’t make decision after decision without paying a biological price. This ‘decision fatigue’ is different from ordinary physical fatigue, people are not conscious of being tired, but nevertheless they are low on energy. The more choices one makes throughout the day, the harder it becomes for the brain, and eventually it looks for shortcuts: either to act impulsively instead of expending the energy to think through the possible results, or the ultimate energy saver: do nothing. Avoiding a decision often creates bigger problems in the long run, but for the moment it eases the mental strain.

evidence.quote: A widely recognised legend tells us that in Gordium (in what is now Turkey) in the fourth century BC an oxcart was roped to a pole with a complex knot. It was said that the first person to untie it would become the king of Asia. Unfortunately, the knot proved impossible to untie. The story continues that when confronted with this problem, rather than deliberating on how to untie the Gordian knot. Alexander, the famous ruler of the Greeks in the ancient world, simply took out his sword and cut it in two – then went on to conquer Asia. Ever since the notion of a ‘Gordian solution’ has referred to the attractiveness of a simple answer to an otherwise intractable problem.

27.explanation: Cắt nút thắt minh họa giải pháp đơn giản cho vấn đề khó.

evidence.quote: Among researchers in the psychology of decision making, however, such solutions have traditionally held little appeal. In particular, the ‘conflict model’ of decision making proposed by psychologists Irving Janis and Leon Mann in their 1977 book, Decision Making, argued that a complex decision-making process is essential for guarding individuals and groups from the peril of ‘group-think’. Decisions made without thoroughly canvassing, surveying, weighing, examining and reexamining relevant information and options would be suboptimal and often disastrous. One foreign affair decision made by a well-known US political leader in the 1960s is typically held us as an example of the perils of inadequate thought, whereas his successful handling of a water crisis is cited as an example of the advantages of careful deliberation. However, examination of these historical events by Peter Suedfield, a psychologist at the University of British Columbia, and Roderick Kramer, a psychologist at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, found little difference in the two decision-making processes; both crises required and received complex consideration by the political administration, but later only the second one was deemed to be the effective.

28.explanation: Mô hình yêu cầu xem xét kỹ mọi dữ kiện và lựa chọn liên quan.

evidence.quote: In general, however, organizational and political science offers little evidence that complex decisions fare better than simpler ones. In fact, a growing body of work suggests that in many situations simply ‘snap’ decisions with being routinely superior to more complex ones – an idea that gained widespread public appeal with Malcolm Gladwell’s best-selling book Blink (2005).

29.explanation: Nghiên cứu mới cho rằng quyết định tức thì thường tốt hơn.

evidence.quote: An article by Ap Dijksterhuis of the University of Amsterdam and his colleagues, ‘On Making the Right Choice: the Deliberation-without-attention Effect’, runs very much in the spirit of Gladwell’s influential text. Its core argument is that to be effective, conscious (deliberative) decision making requires cognitive resources. Because increasingly complex decisions place increasing strain on those resources, the quality of our decisions declines as their complexity increases. In short, complex decisions overrun our cognitive powers. On the other hand, unconscious decision making (what the author refer to as ‘deliberation without attention’) requires no cognitive resources, so task complexity does not degrade effectiveness. The seemingly counterintuitive conclusion is that although conscious thought enhances simple decisions, the opposite holds true for more complex decisions.

30.explanation: Việc phức tạp quá tải tài nguyên nhận thức khi cân nhắc có ý thức.

evidence.quote: Dijksterhuis reports four Simple but elegant studies supporting this argument. In one, participants assessed the quality of four hypothetical cars by considering either four attributes (a simple task) or 12 attributes (a complex task). Among participants who considered four attributes, those who were allowed to engage in undistracted deliberative thought did better at discriminating between the best and worst cars. Those who were distracted and thus unable to deliberate had to rely on their unconscious thinking and did less well. The opposite pattern emerged when people considered 12 criteria. In this case, conscious deliberation led to inferior discrimination and poor decisions.

31.explanation: Bài chọn xe đơn giản cho kết quả tốt hơn khi được tập trung.

evidence.quote: In another study, Dijksterhuis surveyed people shopping for clothes (‘simple’ products) and furniture (‘complex’ products). Compared with those who said they had deliberated long and hard, shoppers who bought with little conscious deliberation felt less happy with their simple clothing purchase but happier with the complex furniture purchases. Deliberation without attention actually produced better results as the decisions became more complex.

evidence.quote: Other street artworks have a far less direct connection to the street, which raises the question of whether street art must be physically in the street. The artist Blu created Muto, a fascinating piece of animation that uses the street as a drawing board. Blu painted characters in his distinctive style on various street surfaces, took a photograph, shifted the character slightly by painting over his previous image, took another photograph, and so on. He then joined the images together to create a video with added sound effects. The result is a kind of real-life animation in which human-like figures appear to walk along walls, crawl under windows, and kick over logs; they lose their heads, expand, split in half, and multiply. One really must see it to believe it. Another example: Invader's mosaics are placed all over various cities, but the finished product is normally a map that details the whereabouts of each work. Invader prints the maps and distributes them in the 'invaded' city. The Paris and Los Angeles invasions are detailed in books and sold on Invader's website. These maps, and Muto, are arguably street art, even though they are not physically located in the street.

14.explanation: Video Muto và bản đồ Invader có thể là street art ngoài đường phố.

evidence.quote: What is street art? We have all seen it but maybe did not recognize it as art. Street art can be graffiti (scribbled names), or murals (large paintings on walls). It is surely therefore just art placed on the street, where the 'street' is taken in a very broad sense to mean, roughly, an urban space where anyone can go. However, this common sense answer cannot be right. In art markets around the world, paintings are often displayed in the street to attract potential customers, but this does not make them street art. Another answer is that street art is made somewhere else and subsequently placed in the street. This is true of some works, but as we will see, in many cases the street is employed in the production of the art. It does not help to add that the art must be in the street for at least a certain length of time. Street art includes works that range from the very short-lived – a matter of minutes, to much longer-lasting – a matter of years.

15.explanation: Tác phẩm có thể tồn tại vài phút hoặc nhiều năm.

evidence.quote: It cannot be a necessary or sufficient condition that street art is art-in-the-street. Still, it obviously has some strong connection to the street. A different suggestion is that it is art that employs the street as an artistic resource. Now, there are different kinds of artistic resources. One kind of artistic resource is the physical material artists use to create their works. Just as painters use canvas, paint, frames, galleries, and walls, street artists use elements of the street. The subway and its brief shots of city air are literally part of Harris's sculptures: the street is the drawing board for Blu's animation: doorways, windows, sidewalks, signposts, rooftops -all are used to create street art. Another kind of artistic resource is the context in which the work is displayed. Some artists use the gallery, studio, or museum; street artists use the street. So perhaps an artwork is street art if, and only if, its creator uses the street as an artistic resource in at least one of these ways.

16.explanation: Đoạn D liệt kê canvas, sơn, khung và gallery.

evidence.quote: Josh Allen Harris creates inflatable creatures out of see-through plastic material and tapes them to subway air ducts on the sidewalks of New York City. When a subway train passes, air shoots out of the ducts and inflates the animals, casting them into a brief and frenzied existence. The inflatable sculptures last about as long as it takes for an average-sized chain of subway cars to zoom by. At the other extreme are the works of an artist known as 'Stikman'. One of Stikman's projects involves sticking little thermoplastic stickmen on the roadway in the middle of the street (normally in crosswalks). Unless they are deliberately destroyed, they will be there as long as the crosswalk is. The work of Invader, another street artist, is equally lasting. With powerful glue, he affixes mosaics (art that uses many tiny pieces of different colored materials to form a larger picture) depicting digital-style space creatures to various surfaces.

evidence.quote: This definition gets something right, but it is too inclusive. Posters and billboards use the street as an artistic resource – but they are not street art. So what is the distinction? The answer lies in the fact that street art's meaning is severely compromised when removed from the street. The artist C. Finley beautifies rugged steel dumpsters (large metal rubbish containers) by covering them with pretty wallpaper. That the wallpaper is on a dumpster is what makes it noteworthy. By covering dumpsters with such homey material, Finley draws attention to the fact that the street is also a kind of living room. Her work reveals that the elements of our shared public spaces need not be so uninviting. Wallpaper alone is merely pretty. Wallpaper on a dumpster: that is street art. Therefore, the material use of the street is internal to the meaning of street art. In contrast, the meaning of an advertisement does not change if it is removed from the street. Finley's wallpaper is removed from the dumpster, or if the wallpapered dumpster is placed in a gallery, the meaning of the work will be severely compromised, if not entirely destroyed.

evidence.quote: What is street art? We have all seen it but maybe did not recognize it as art. Street art can be graffiti (scribbled names), or murals (large paintings on walls). It is surely therefore just art placed on the street, where the 'street' is taken in a very broad sense to mean, roughly, an urban space where anyone can go. However, this common sense answer cannot be right. In art markets around the world, paintings are often displayed in the street to attract potential customers, but this does not make them street art. Another answer is that street art is made somewhere else and subsequently placed in the street. This is true of some works, but as we will see, in many cases the street is employed in the production of the art. It does not help to add that the art must be in the street for at least a certain length of time. Street art includes works that range from the very short-lived – a matter of minutes, to much longer-lasting – a matter of years.

evidence.quote: Other street artworks have a far less direct connection to the street, which raises the question of whether street art must be physically in the street. The artist Blu created Muto, a fascinating piece of animation that uses the street as a drawing board. Blu painted characters in his distinctive style on various street surfaces, took a photograph, shifted the character slightly by painting over his previous image, took another photograph, and so on. He then joined the images together to create a video with added sound effects. The result is a kind of real-life animation in which human-like figures appear to walk along walls, crawl under windows, and kick over logs; they lose their heads, expand, split in half, and multiply. One really must see it to believe it. Another example: Invader's mosaics are placed all over various cities, but the finished product is normally a map that details the whereabouts of each work. Invader prints the maps and distributes them in the 'invaded' city. The Paris and Los Angeles invasions are detailed in books and sold on Invader's website. These maps, and Muto, are arguably street art, even though they are not physically located in the street.

evidence.quote: Deserts cover more than one third of the Earth's land surface, but only quite a small proportion of desert area is sandy – the rest is bare rock or rock fragments. As well as hot deserts, such as the Sahara and Kalahari in Africa, there are also temperate and cold deserts, of which many, such as the Gobi in Asia, owe their origin to being many thousands of kilometres from the oceans, so the rain-bearing winds never reach them.

1.explanation: Nhiều hoang mạc ôn đới và lạnh cách biển hàng nghìn kilomet.

evidence.quote: Deserts are extreme and infertile environments where few species of plants and animals are able to survive. However, this means that competition between desert species is reduced, and for some, life in such an environment is actually easier than fighting for survival in environments where basic resources are plentiful.

2.explanation: Cạnh tranh thấp khiến một số loài sống dễ hơn ở nơi màu mỡ.

evidence.quote: The vegetation in all deserts shows extreme adaptation to suit the dry conditions. Smallness of size, leaves reduced to thin spines, long, deep roots, and the ability to grow very quickly at the start of rains are some of the most useful adaptations. The seeds of many desert plants can remain inactive for up to five years, awaiting the occurrence of damp conditions suitable for growth. Other species have adapted to the long, dry spells by storing water in enlarged, fat stems. These are the so-called succulent plants, of which the cacti of the Americas are the best-known examples. The most spectacular cactus is the barrel cactus, which was traditionally used as a water reserve by the Native Americans. Elsewhere in the world, the Euphorbia group of plants predominates in deserts. The stems of these plants are filled with a sticky substance which resists evaporation.

3.explanation: Không nói quan hệ tiến hóa giữa cacti và nhóm cây nơi khác.

evidence.quote: Animal life in deserts is surprisingly varied. Most animals that inhabit them are active primarily at night, or during the brief periods of early morning and late afternoon, when the heat is not as strong. During the day they remain in cooler underground burrows, or in the shade of overhanging rocks. Rodents, snakes, lizards, spiders and insects are the main animal types. There are a few larger animals and birds too.

4.explanation: Đa số hoạt động đêm hoặc lúc mát và trú ban ngày.

evidence.quote: Common characteristics of desert animals are large skin flaps (particularly large ears) from which heat can be lost, an absence of sweat glands, and an ability to lose a large proportion of body weight in the dry season.

5.explanation: Tai lớn giúp tỏa nhiệt.

evidence.quote: One animal which is especially well adapted to life in desert conditions is the camel. Each foot has two toes which are joined by a wide piece of skin that can be spread out, which prevents the animals from sinking into soft sand. The eyes are protected from sand by heavy lashes, while the nostrils can be closed to exclude sand when the animal breathes in. The fatty humps on their back act as food reserves in case of shortage.

evidence.quote: The camel's well-known ability to go for long periods without drinking – for over a week while travelling long distances – is due to a number of adaptations designed to save water. Camels do not start to sweat until the temperature reaches 40°C; heat accumulated in the body during the day is given off in the cool of the night. Camels can survive a water loss of about 40% of their body weight without suffering damage, and the water content of the urine is minimised by the kidneys. Following a prolonged period without water, camels have been known to drink over 100 litres in a matter of minutes.

evidence.quote: The camel plays a major role in the life of nomadic societies living in the desert, such as the Touareg of north Africa. At the start of the seventh century, Arabs started moving into the coastal regions of Africa, pushing the Touareg into the Sahara Desert. Here the Touareg took on the role of trans-Saharan camel traders, travelling across the desert plains from one destination to the next, and setting up tents along the way. They once travelled the desert in great numbers, but they have now been reduced to small groups. Today, the Touareg are still known for camel trading, but are also involved in rearing cattle and producing metal work. Their crafted swords, jewellery and leather work have become sought-after items in other parts of the world. In addition, traditional Touareg music is now played at international festivals. In these ways, people have become much more aware of these desert nomads and their way of life.

evidence.quote: As society has developed, the role of design has shifted and changed in scope, scale and technique. For most of human history, products were designed and made by individuals for their own use or by craftsmen who made a limited number of items to sell or barter. After hundreds of years of this craft-based production of goods, the industrial revolution in the 19th century created particular occupations to support industrial manufacture. Design filled a necessary and increasingly important function in the mass production of goods. Designers in industry were given titles such as engineer, architect, draftsman, chemist and so on. However, what defined these new designers more than any other thing was their ability to imagine products that could be made in quantity through large-scale production, and specify realistic ways to create them.

evidence.quote: For mass production, the risk of serious flaws in the finished item must be removed as far as possible. Therefore, with the shift from craft to industrial manufacture, the process of creation shifted in great part from the actual maker of the product to its designer, the person who was best able to anticipate and thus avoid potential imperfections before the goods were actually made. Much of the judgement, dexterity and care was therefore manifested in thought and intention at the design stage, rather than during its manufacture.

31.explanation: Trách nhiệm tránh lỗi chuyển từ người làm sang người thiết kế.

evidence.quote: As the scale of production of modern industrial goods has increased in our society, the choices and decisions made by designers have increased in importance. Now, these decisions often have global impact. For example, an architect who specifies a particular type of aluminum-framed window for a skyscraper is making a decision not only about cost, appearance, usability, strength and safety, but also about an entire supply chain that provides those windows, from the raw materials needed to make the components through the various steps in the manufacturing, marketing and shipping of the product. The architect's specifications play a role in shaping demands placed on international mineral mining and petroleum production companies, glassmakers and trucking companies, to name but a few. The actions of all of these players will in turn affect the people working in mining, in factories, and many other points along the supply chain. They will also touch the lives of people in communities in which the mines, factories, and trucks are located or moving through, as well as of those who live around the landfill where the windows may end up as rubbish perhaps many years in the future. The designer's reach is vast. There are many effects, both intended and unintended, that spread from the choices the designer originally makes.

32.explanation: Lựa chọn thiết kế ảnh hưởng rộng suốt chuỗi cung ứng.

evidence.quote: This is known as the 'ripple effect' — when one action causes a series of other actions to happen. Until the late 20th century, designers did not have to think much about this because their role used to be simpler. The designer was usually responsible for not much more than creating products that looked good and that met the specific financial and functional requirements of the problem at hand. Today however, design is increasingly being re-defined in light of issues such as climate change, shifts in ecosystem structure and function, and water scarcity, as well as human rights violations, among other issues. An acute awareness of the ripple effect is a result of growing understanding of impacts of products and of the need for companies to be accountable for these impacts — the positive and negative results — throughout their operations and supply chains.

33.explanation: Doanh nghiệp phải quan tâm tác động môi trường và nhân quyền ngoài sản phẩm.

evidence.quote: Many corporate leaders are now showing an active interest in the design process of the goods their companies make or sell. This increased interest is due to a range of reasons, not least of which is the recognition that it is best to be ahead of potential government regulation, as well as activist pressures and public relations disasters. This perception also means that companies hiring design firms are more aware of the need for sustainability —the goal of not harming the environment or depleting natural resources. They must support the long-term ecological balance and recognise the importance of integrating these issues into core strategy, operations, and products. It will be up to the designer to make sure these factors are incorporated into new products that can be successfully marketed.

34.explanation: Lãnh đạo muốn đi trước quy định, áp lực hoạt động và khủng hoảng hình ảnh.

evidence.quote: In the future, it will be increasingly necessary for the designer to recognise that we must use far fewer resources to meet far more people's needs since many resources are already in short supply. How can people's perceived needs and desires be reshaped and addressed so that what they want can be achieved? How can the designer put principles of sustainability into practice? Fortunately, work has already begun on this. Visionary individuals and organisations are making strides in design approaches, such as the 'green design' movement, which attempt to ensure that design uses more natural products sensitively. Similar work is under way on providing guidance for the production of raw materials and manufacturing that considers human rights issues, most notably including 'fair trade'; this ensures that workers and producers of raw materials receive a reasonable price for their product. Yet numerous challenges remain, ranging from fully incorporating social goals, such as improving the conditions of the workers who are perhaps growing, digging up or otherwise providing raw materials, to assessing the ecological friendliness of materials.

evidence.quote: When the 11 ships of the First Fleet arrived in Australia from England in 1788, they brought not only convicts, soldiers, plants and animals from Britain to the new colony of New South Wales, but also the colony’s first printing press and first books. These books were not those of a public library, but the small collections of individuals, or books of the type of learning thought to be necessary in the establishment of a new colony — law books, religious books, books of science and navigation. But as Peter Biskup points out in his book Libraries in Australia, the most important thing brought to Australia in the First Fleet which impacted on the development of libraries was the idea that libraries would be an important asset for the colony.

1.explanation: First Fleet mang máy in và sách.

evidence.quote: The first, although unsuccessful, attempt to establish a public library in the new colony of New South Wales was through an appeal to the British public by the Reverend Samuel Marsden. In 1809 he began to collect contributions so that he could set up a library of ‘carefully selected books … suited to the poor settlers employed in agriculture, the soldiers and the convicts’.

2.explanation: Marsden muốn lập thư viện công cộng.

evidence.quote: In 1821 a catalogue of books in the personal libraries belonging to private citizens in the colony was compiled. From these, a number of libraries began to emerge. The 1820s saw the setting up of subscription libraries, where the user had to pay to borrow books, and by the 1830s the introduction of Schools of Arts, and Mechanics’ Institutes had further added to the number of libraries available to the people of the colony. The first of these in Australia was the Van Diemen’s Land Mechanics’ Institute, Hobart, which opened in that city in 1827. Others followed in Melbourne and other Australian cities and towns. By 1900 Australia supported 1,000 Mechanics’ Institutes each with memberships of between 100 and 200 people. Most of these institutes had fewer than 1,000 books.

3.explanation: Thư viện trả phí mượn xuất hiện thập niên 1820.

evidence.quote: Free municipal libraries began to appear in Australia in the 1850s, as did central public libraries — which largely went on to become the State Libraries. Parliamentary libraries were established to support the work of state parliaments, and a Commonwealth Parliamentary Library was set up in Melbourne in 1901 to support the new Commonwealth Parliament. In 1923 the Commonwealth Parliamentary Library became the Commonwealth National Library, the precursor to the National Library of Australia, which became a separate entity under its own Act of Parliament in 1960.

evidence.quote: When the 11 ships of the First Fleet arrived in Australia from England in 1788, they brought not only convicts, soldiers, plants and animals from Britain to the new colony of New South Wales, but also the colony’s first printing press and first books. These books were not those of a public library, but the small collections of individuals, or books of the type of learning thought to be necessary in the establishment of a new colony — law books, religious books, books of science and navigation. But as Peter Biskup points out in his book Libraries in Australia, the most important thing brought to Australia in the First Fleet which impacted on the development of libraries was the idea that libraries would be an important asset for the colony.

8.explanation: Có sách luật, tôn giáo, khoa học và hàng hải cần cho thuộc địa.

evidence.quote: The first, although unsuccessful, attempt to establish a public library in the new colony of New South Wales was through an appeal to the British public by the Reverend Samuel Marsden. In 1809 he began to collect contributions so that he could set up a library of ‘carefully selected books … suited to the poor settlers employed in agriculture, the soldiers and the convicts’.

9.explanation: Nỗ lực thư viện công cộng đầu tiên không thành.

evidence.quote: The ‘School of Arts’ movement had begun in Britain in the beginning of the 19th century and produced a worldwide response. The first School of Arts opened in Edinburgh, Scotland in 1821, with others opening in Glasgow, Scotland and London, England in 1823. In Australia, the term ‘Mechanics’ Institute’ was popular, but the institutions so named could also be known as Schools of Arts. These schools or institutes were places where people, mainly working class men, could go and hear lectures of use to them in their practical work, or access a library of books, and so improve themselves. Mechanics’ Institutes were very often supported by the colonial governments — usually by land grants and cash assistance. They were particularly popular in country areas where their role often went far beyond their ‘library’ function to providing a general focus for the community’s cultural activities. Because of this important role and because of the support of the colonial governments, Mechanics’ Institute buildings were frequently quite imposing, and today form an important part of Australia’s built heritage. The Tenterfield School of Arts, Tenterfield, New South Wales, was the venue in which the statesman Henry Parkes made a famous speech, which is now seen as the first step towards the creation of the nation of Australia.

evidence.quote: Libraries today are much more than storehouses for books. Technologies like the internet mean libraries now also provide readers with gateways to the online world, and librarians are the finders of knowledge in cyber space as well as in their own stacks. The internet also makes the National Library of Australia’s heritage — the vast collection of books, manuscripts, photos, posters and leaflets — more accessible to more Australians. As the former Minister for Communications, Information Technology and the Arts, Senator Richard Alston stated, libraries are no longer simply storehouses of information and resources, but are actually gateways to information from all over the world.

evidence.quote: The adolescent must adjust to a new physical sense of self. At no other time since birth does an individual undergo such profound physical changes as during early adolescence. Puberty is marked by sudden rapid growth in height and weight. Also, the young person experiences the emergence and accentuation of those physical traits that make the person a boy or a girl. The young person looks less like a child and more like a physically mature adult. The effect of this rapid change is that mid-adolescents are body-conscious, and their concerns are directed towards their opposite-sexed peers.

1.explanation: Giữa tuổi thiếu niên chú ý cơ thể và bạn khác giới.

evidence.quote: The adolescent must establish adult vocational goals. As part of the process of establishing a personal identity, the adolescent must also begin the process of focusing on the question, ‘What do you plan to be when you grow up?’ Mid-adolescents must identify, at least at a preliminary level, what their adult vocational goals are and how they intend to achieve them.

2.explanation: Mid-adolescents bắt đầu xác định mục tiêu nghề nghiệp.

evidence.quote: The adolescent must develop stable and productive peer relationships. Although peer interaction is not unique to adolescence, it seems to hit a peak of importance during early adolescence. Certainly by late adolescence or early adulthood the need for peer approval has diminished. This degree to which an adolescent is able to make friends and have an accepting peer group, though, is a major indicator of how well the adolescent will adjust in other areas of social and psychological development. Early adolescence is also a period of intense conformity to peers. ‘Fitting in’, not being different, and being accepted seem somehow pressing to this age group. The worst possibility, from the view of the young teen, is to be seen by peers as ‘different’.

3.explanation: Đầu thiếu niên đặc biệt cần giống và được bạn chấp nhận.

evidence.quote: The adolescent must develop a personal sense of identity. Prior to adolescence, one’s identity is an extension of one’s parents’ identity. During the early adolescent years a young person begins to recognise their uniqueness and to establish themselves as separate individuals, independent of their parents. As such, one must reconsider the answer to the question, ‘What does it mean to be me?’ or ‘Who am I?’

4.explanation: Nhận diện bản thân độc lập gia đình bắt đầu ở early adolescent years.

evidence.quote: The adolescent must develop increased impulse control and behavioural maturity. In their shift to adulthood, most young people engage in one or more behaviours that place them at physical, social, or educational risk. Risky behaviours are sufficiently pervasive among adolescents to suggest that risk-taking may be a normal developmental process of middle adolescence. Gradually adolescents develop a set of behavioural self-controls through which they assess which behaviours are acceptable and adult-like.

6.explanation: Chấp nhận rủi ro được xem bình thường ở middle adolescence.

evidence.quote: Some years ago, Professor Robert Havighurst of the University of Chicago, USA, proposed that stages in human development can best be thought of in terms of the developmental ‘tasks’ that are part of the normal transition. He identified ten developmental tasks associated with the adolescent transition. Each of the Havighurst tasks can also be seen as elements of the overall sense of self that adolescents carry with them as they move towards and into young adulthood. Adolescents do not progress through these multiple developmental tasks separately; at any given time they may be dealing with several.

7.explanation: Mười nhiệm vụ phản ánh ý thức về bản thân đang phát triển.

evidence.quote: The adolescent must adjust to increased cognitive demands at school. Adults see high school in part as a place where adolescents prepare for adult roles and responsibilities and in part as preparatory for further education. School curricula are frequently dominated by the inclusion of more abstract, demanding material, regardless of whether the adolescents have achieved formal thought. Since not all adolescents make the intellectual transition at the same rate, demands for abstract thinking prior to the achievement of that ability may be frustrating.

8.explanation: Chương trình trung học bao gồm nội dung khó và trừu tượng hơn.

evidence.quote: The adolescent must adopt a personal value system. During adolescence, as teens develop increasingly complex knowledge systems, they also adopt an integrated set of values and morals. During the early stages of moral development, parents provide their child with a structured set of rules of what is right and wrong, what is acceptable and unacceptable. Eventually the adolescent must assess the parent’s values as they come into conflict with values expressed by peers and other segments of society. To reconcile differences, the adolescent restructures those beliefs into a personal ideology.

10.explanation: Thiếu niên tái cấu trúc giá trị thành hệ tư tưởng riêng.

evidence.quote: The adolescent must adjust to new intellectual abilities. In addition to a sudden spurt in physical growth, adolescents experience a sudden increase in their ability to think about their world. As a normal part of maturity, they are able to think about more things. However, they are also able to conceive of their world with a new level of awareness. Before adolescence, children’s thinking is dominated by a need to have a concrete example for any problem that they solve; their thinking is constrained to what is real and physical. During adolescence, young people begin to recognise and understand abstractions. The growth in ability to deal with abstractions accelerates during the middle stages of adolescence.

11.explanation: Trước thiếu niên tư duy còn phụ thuộc ví dụ cụ thể.

evidence.quote: The adolescent must develop expanded verbal skills to accommodate more complex concepts and tasks. Their limited language of childhood is no longer adequate. As their conceptual development may outstrip their verbal development, adolescents may appear less competent than they really are.

evidence.quote: Traditionally, scholars have studied literature by intensively looking at individual written texts or perhaps comparing a few such texts. However, today, with the use of advanced computer technology, some researchers are aggregating and analysing massive quantities of information including words from thousands of texts. Franco Moretti, founder of the Literary Lab at Stanford University in the USA, is one such researcher. He tackles literary problems by scientific means: hypothesis-testing, computational modelling and quantitative analysis. He advocates understanding literature not by studying individual texts, but by applying rigorous scientific methods to study an enormous number of texts collectively. Only in that way, Moretti argues, can you identify broad literary patterns and currents. A good example of this approach can be found in the work of a team of researchers at Dartmouth College in the USA, led by Professor Daniel Rockmore. The Dartmouth group set out to study the evolution of the literary styles of authors writing in English between the 16th and the 20th centuries, looking at literary trends across many works. The research used data from 7,733 digitised books written by 537 authors available from the Project Gutenberg library.

14.explanation: Phân tích số lượng văn bản lớn giúp tìm xu hướng chung.

evidence.quote: The Dartmouth researchers focused on the usage of ‘content-free’ words like prepositions (e.g. ‘of’, ‘in’, ‘to’), conjunctions (e.g. ‘and’, ‘but’), and articles (e.g. ‘the’, ‘a’, ‘an’) which, Professor Rockmore explained, are useful for stylistic analysis because they do not convey meaning. While content words can yield data about subject matter, content-free words can provide data for the analysis of literary style. Professor Rockmore says that content-free words form the ‘glue’ of language: they carry little or no meaning on their own but form the bridge between words that do convey meaning and thus provide useful stylistic fingerprints for literary characteristics.

15.explanation: Từ không mang nội dung được chọn để phân tích phong cách.

evidence.quote: The Dartmouth researchers found that the writing of authors in the 18th and 19th centuries was stylistically similar, and was strongly affected by the writing of their predecessors from previous centuries. Therefore 18th- and 19th-century authors displayed a remarkably similar choice of words, phrasing, meaning and grammar. This resulted in significant stylistic stability, with styles remaining relatively unchanged for extensive periods. However, authors writing in the 20th century were most affected by other 20th-century writers. In other words, the past seems to be exerting a diminishing stylistic influence on the present. If one believes that writing style is significantly related to popular speech, then the diminishing importance of the past might be traced to the speed with which spoken communication is changing today. According to Professor Rockmore, another reason for this may be that because of the huge number of new books now coming on the market each year, people devote less of their reading time to the ‘classics’ and are thus less affected by them.

16.explanation: Nguồn sách mới lớn làm đọc kinh điển ít và giảm ảnh hưởng quá khứ.

evidence.quote: The prize-winning American novelist Lionel Shriver agrees that her own writing style has not been very much affected by older literary works, and suggests that this is likely to apply to other modern writers as well. She confesses that while she devoured classics in her teens and 20s, she now reads contemporary fiction almost exclusively. With all the other things she does, like writing book reviews, she doesn’t often get around to the classics. She says, ‘I’ve discovered that I don’t have the patience any longer – for the long philosophical digressions, for example. I bet I’m not alone in this reduced tolerance for the stylistic traditions of the past.’

17.explanation: Shriver kể trải nghiệm đọc cá nhân ủng hộ phát hiện.

evidence.quote: While digital literary analysis has been hailed by some scholars as an opportunity to revitalise the field of literary studies, others remain unconvinced. Dartmouth English professor Aden Evens fears that the new methods of analysis provided by digitisation will appeal to different people, including university administrators who to some extent control or at least help decide on the funding of academic research. Evens continues, ‘What I am worried about is that we are asked to set aside what most distinguishes the humanities – our ability to perform critiques of ambiguity – and instead we are being asked to supplant it with a view of knowledge that promotes certainty, statistical or numerical style analyses, absolute and clear distinctions.’

18.explanation: Evens lo phân tích số lấn át năng lực phê bình sự mơ hồ.

evidence.quote: Other scholars feel that quantitative methodologies will never replace the more usual ways of studying literary texts. In interpreting what the numbers mean, a literary scholar has to bring in all the knowledge of literature and authors that is applied in customary literary studies. Computer-based interpretation of texts, however, can provide opportunities to ask new questions about literature. According to James Hughes, a member of the Dartmouth team, researchers using computational tools do not claim to employ the ‘best’ approach to literature. ‘The point is really,’ writes Hughes, ‘that traditional analyses that take into account the intangible or unquantifiable factors can benefit from the addition of quantitative evidence.’

19.explanation: Hughes đề nghị kết hợp định lượng với truyền thống.

evidence.quote: Many linguists predict that at least half the world's 6,000 or so languages will be dead or dying by the year 2050. Languages are becoming extinct at twice the rate of endangered mammals and four times the rate of endangered birds. If this trend continues, the world of the future could be dominated by a dozen or fewer languages. Michael Krauss, director of the Alaska Native Language Center, suggests that as many as 90 per cent of languages could be dying or extinct by 2100. According to Krauss, 20 to 40 per cent of languages are already declining, and only 5 to 10 per cent are 'safe' in the sense of being widely spoken or having official status. If people 'become wise and turn it around', Krauss says, the number of dead or dying languages could perhaps be 50 per cent by 2100.

27.explanation: Krauss nói hành động khôn ngoan có thể giảm tỷ lệ mất ngôn ngữ.

evidence.quote: The definition of a healthy language is one that acquires new speakers. No matter how many adults use the language, if it isn't passed to the next generation, its future as a living language is in jeopardy. A language may continue to exist for a long time as a second or ceremonial language, but it is on the way out as soon as children stop learning it. Although language extinction is sad for the people involved, why should the rest of us care? Replacing a minor language with a more widespread one may even seem like a good thing, allowing people to communicate with each other more easily. But it isn't. Language diversity is as important as biological diversity.

28.explanation: Ngôn ngữ bắt đầu chết khi trẻ không học nữa.

evidence.quote: Andrew Woodfield, director of the Centre for Theories of Language and Learning in Bristol, England, suggested in a seminar on language conservation that people do not know 'exactly what riches are hidden inside the less-studied languages'. Woodfield compares one argument for conserving unstudied endangered plants — that they may be medically valuable —with the argument for conserving endangered languages. 'We have inductive evidence based on past studies of well-known languages that there will be riches, even though we do not know what they will be. By allowing languages to die out, the human race is destroying things it doesn't understand,' he argues.

29.explanation: Mất ngôn ngữ là phá hủy tri thức chưa hiểu rõ.

evidence.quote: As Krauss aptly expresses it, the web of languages is a 'microcosm of highly specialized information. Every language has its own take on the world. One language is not simply a different set of words for the same things.' He further argues that just as we depend on biological complexity for our physical survival, we depend on linguistic complexity for our cultural survival.

30.explanation: Đa dạng sinh học giúp sống thể chất, ngôn ngữ giúp sống văn hóa.

evidence.quote: Some language loss, like species loss, is natural and predictable. Just as plants and animals have appeared and disappeared over the millennia, languages evolve, grow, spread, and eventually dwindle and die. Sometimes they're replaced by their 'descendant' languages, as Italian gradually replaced Latin in Europe. Other times they're forced out, as the ancient Etruscan language was when Latin speakers overran the Italian peninsula.

31.explanation: Latin, Italian và Etruscan minh họa thay đổi ngôn ngữ tự nhiên.

evidence.quote: Language extinction is accelerating today for some of the same reasons as species extinction — population pressures and the spread of industrialization. The global economy often forces small, unindustrialized communities to choose between their traditional language and participation in the larger world. Sometimes more global languages coexist with the local language. More often, they eventually replace it as older speakers die and younger ones adopt the more useful tongue. Even strong national languages have some worries. The European Union, for instance, is increasingly concerned that English will eventually replace some European languages, since it's the only language many Europeans have in common.

32.explanation: Cần giao tiếp kinh tế rộng hơn thường thay thế tiếng địa phương.

evidence.quote: The Cornish language, once spoken in southwestern England, expired in 1777 when its last living speaker died, but has made a comeback. With the help of surviving documents, a small group of descendants of Cornish speakers began to learn their language and speak it to their children. Now, about 2,000 people speak Cornish. Other examples of resuscitated languages are Welsh and Navajo. Speakers revitalized their dying languages through 'immersion' high schools where students use their ancestral language every day. Both languages have grown in numbers of speakers over the past few decades.

33.explanation: Học sinh trung học học qua hòa nhập hằng ngày.

evidence.quote: The Native California Network is a program that teams fluent speakers of native Californian languages with apprentice speakers. The apprentices immerse themselves in conversations with the 'master' speakers and meet with groups for weekly conversation. It has had an effect. Speakers of one native Californian language, Hupa, for instance, have succeeded in getting Hupa to count as a foreign language for college entrance requirements. Even a few such language apprenticeships may help avert the wholesale extinction of minor languages.

34.explanation: Hupa được chấp nhận làm ngoại ngữ xét tuyển đại học.

evidence.quote: The definition of a healthy language is one that acquires new speakers. No matter how many adults use the language, if it isn't passed to the next generation, its future as a living language is in jeopardy. A language may continue to exist for a long time as a second or ceremonial language, but it is on the way out as soon as children stop learning it. Although language extinction is sad for the people involved, why should the rest of us care? Replacing a minor language with a more widespread one may even seem like a good thing, allowing people to communicate with each other more easily. But it isn't. Language diversity is as important as biological diversity.
