evidence.quote: Stephen Wurm, in 'The World's Languages in Danger', tells the story of one medical cure that depended on knowledge of a traditional language. In Northern Australia there was an outbreak of severe skin ulcers that resisted conventional treatment. Aborigines, descendants of the original inhabitants of Australia, who were acquainted with a nurse working on the case, told her about a lotion derived from a local medicinal plant. The lotion healed the ulcers. This incident and similar ones have resulted in a general search for medicinal plants known to aboriginal people through their languages and traditional cultures. Most Australian languages are dying. When they go, the medical knowledge stored in them will go, too.

evidence.quote: Language extinction is accelerating today for some of the same reasons as species extinction — population pressures and the spread of industrialization. The global economy often forces small, unindustrialized communities to choose between their traditional language and participation in the larger world. Sometimes more global languages coexist with the local language. More often, they eventually replace it as older speakers die and younger ones adopt the more useful tongue. Even strong national languages have some worries. The European Union, for instance, is increasingly concerned that English will eventually replace some European languages, since it's the only language many Europeans have in common.

evidence.quote: The Native California Network is a program that teams fluent speakers of native Californian languages with apprentice speakers. The apprentices immerse themselves in conversations with the 'master' speakers and meet with groups for weekly conversation. It has had an effect. Speakers of one native Californian language, Hupa, for instance, have succeeded in getting Hupa to count as a foreign language for college entrance requirements. Even a few such language apprenticeships may help avert the wholesale extinction of minor languages.

evidence.quote: Humans are born time travellers: we can relive events that happened long ago or imagine ourselves in the future. Clues about different kinds of memory can be discovered from research conducted on people with certain brain injuries that cause them to forget autobiographical details without forgetting the information they picked up along the way. A man known as KC in the scientific literature, for instance, could play chess with no memory of having ever played it before. He could also remember sentences psychologists taught him without any memory of the lessons. KC had lost what psychologists now call ‘episodic memory’. Dr Endel Tulving, a Canadian psychologist, defined episodic memory as the ability to recall the details of personal experiences: what happened, where it happened, when it happened and so on. Dr Tulving argued that episodic memory was distinct from other kinds of memory and that it was unique to our species.

14.explanation: Tổn thương của KC giúp mô tả trí nhớ episodic.

evidence.quote: But are humans alone in this respect? Dr Nicola Clayton, of Cambridge University, has performed experiments which test American birds called western scrub jays to see if they met any of the criteria for episodic memory. The jays bury several thousand pieces of food a year and remember the location of each one. Dr Clayton wondered if scrub jays simply remembered the locations, or if they remembered details of the experience of hiding the food. She ran an experiment using two kinds of food: moth larvae and peanuts. Scrub jays prefer larvae to peanuts if the larvae are still fresh. However, if the larvae have been dead for even a few hours, the jays prefer peanuts. Dr Clayton gave the birds a chance to hide both kinds of food in a sandy hiding area. Dr Clayton noted exactly what the birds had hidden and where, and then put the birds in a cage. She later returned the birds to the area where they had hidden the food, in some cases after four hours and in other cases after five days. The time the scrub jays had spent away from their hiding area affected the type of food they looked for. The birds that waited only four hours tended to dig up larvae, while the birds that had to wait for five days passed the larvae by and dug up peanuts instead. To make sure they were not just smelling the rotten larvae and avoiding those spots, Dr Clayton replaced the sand with fresh sand in the hiding area as soon as the birds had hidden the food.

15.explanation: Scrub jays nhớ vị trí và thời gian giấu thức ăn.

evidence.quote: Research with other animals to determine if they are capable of episodic memory has had mixed results. When experimental rats are exploring a maze they seem to be able to recall which kinds of food they encounter along the way. Observation of hummingbirds as they feed appears to show that they remember where and when they visited individual flowers for nectar. Tests using Rhesus monkeys have found that they can remember where they put food, but not how long ago they put it there.

evidence.quote: True episodic memory, argues Dr Thomas Suddendorf of Australia’s Queensland University, involves more than just memory of information. It requires an awareness of the self and an ability to use the past to predict the future. He points to the discovery of stone tools which primitive humans used for killing animals 1.6 million years ago. Scientists assume that primitive humans had to find a way of adding much needed protein to their diet. Paleontologists have determined that some of these tools were moved many kilometres from where they were originally made. ‘If you've just eaten, the only reason you're going to take a tool with you is if you anticipate using it in the future,’ said Dr Suddendorf.

17.explanation: Mang công cụ theo cho thấy người tiền sử dự liệu tương lai.

evidence.quote: Recent brain scanning studies provide physiological support for this link between past and future. Daniel Schacter, a psychologist at Harvard University, studied how brains function as people think about past experiences and imagine the future. When Schacter’s subjects constructed episodic memories, distinct networks of their brains became active, as recorded by brain scans. When they are asked to think about themselves in the future, many parts of the same episodic memory networks become active again, suggesting an inter-connection between the processing of the past and future.

18.explanation: Quét não cho thấy nhớ quá khứ và hình dung tương lai dùng mạng chung.

evidence.quote: Dr Suddendorf’s notions have spurred comparative psychologists to look for evidence that animals can also think ahead. Some studies suggest not. Cebus monkeys, for example, will eat until they are full and throw the rest of the food out of their cage, despite the fact that they will not have anything to eat the next morning. But in other studies, animals show more promise. ‘We tested squirrel monkeys to see if they could anticipate the future, and to our surprise it looks like they could,’ said Dr William Roberts, a comparative psychologist at the University of Western Ontario in Canada. He and his colleagues ran a test in which they gave squirrel monkeys a choice between one or four dates to eat. Not surprisingly, the monkeys took four. But the scientists then began to take away water from the monkeys before they gave them the choice. If the monkeys took four, the scientists kept the water away for three hours. If the monkeys took one, the scientists returned it in half an hour. The monkeys learned to choose one. Though they were not thirsty at the time, they seemed to understand that they would become so in future.

evidence.quote: At the end of STAR, researchers analysed the data. Jeremy Finn of New York University and Charles Achilles of Eastern Michigan University found evidence for 'an array of benefits of small classes'. They calculated that students in smaller classes were outperforming their counterparts in regular-sized classes by the first grade and that this advantage persisted even after students returned to larger classes. They also found that the effect was stronger for black and Hispanic minority groups – a significant finding for policy-makers. Eric Hanushek of Stanford, however, criticises some of STAR's key conclusions. He argues that STAR does not prove that gains persist long after students return to regular classes. It was debatable how much later improvement stemmed from other factors, such as a supportive home. Nor does he accept that the benefits accumulate, with participants widening the gap with their peers in larger classes year by year. Hanushek and others have also shown that during the study too many children moved from regular to small classes, probably because school personnel caved in to parent demands. And Hanushek also asserts that STAR failed to ensure good randomisation of teacher and student assignments. However, these points do not undermine STAR's basic findings.

evidence.quote: Wisconsin's Student Achievement Guarantee in Education (SAGE) was a five-year pilot study to do some of the groundwork for a major project. Class sizes were reduced in only 14 schools, but it was noteworthy for targeting schools at which 30% of the students were below poverty level, compared with California's across-the-board approach. SAGE lowered the average pupil-teacher ratio in kindergarten through third grade to 12-15:1 from 21-25:1. Analysts have studied the results of first-grade students in these schools and similar first-grade students elsewhere and found the results accord with those from STAR. STAR and SAGE have made it hard to argue against reducing class sizes. But the California initiative shows that reductions made with too lite forethought can yield minuscule gains. Administrators need solid information before they can make sensible policy decisions.

evidence.quote: Of all the ideas for improving education, few are as simple or attractive as reducing the number of pupils per teacher. Unlike competing proposals for reform, class-size reductions rarely elicit huge outcries or involve structural change. The testing of educators, by contrast, generally arouses the anger of unions. Similarly, establishing special 'charter' schools involves privileging some schools over others, with the credits provided usually coming out of the budgets of struggling local schools. With its uncomplicated appeal, class-size reduction in the U.S. has lately gone from being a subject of primary academic interest to a policy juggernaut with over twenty states aiming at decreasing class sizes.

evidence.quote: Over the past 35 years, some studies of existing data have produced evidence that smaller classes benefit students, but most of these studies were poorly designed. The exception was the Tennessee study called Project STAR (Student Teacher Achievement Ratio). Frederick Mosteller of Harvard University has called it 'one of the greatest experiments in education in United States history'. Students entering kindergarten were randomly assigned to one of three kinds of classes: a small class of 13 to 17 students, a regular-size class of 22 to 26 or a regular-size class with both a teacher and a full-time teacher's aide. The students remained in whatever category they had been assigned to throughout the third grade, after which they joined a regular classroom in the fourth. To ensure that teaching quality did not differ, teachers were randomly assigned to small and regular-size classrooms. Few teachers received any special training for working with small classes, and there were no new curricular materials.

What is more, the effect did not vary for students of different backgrounds.

evidence.quote: The Kewalo Basin dolphin language studies of the mid-1970s, which were begun by Louis Herman and colleagues, emphasized language comprehension from the start. The researchers, working principally with a bottlenose dolphin named Akeakamai, constructed a sign language in which the gestures of a person's arms and hands corresponded to words. The words referred to objects from Akeakamai's habitat, and what the dolphin could do with them. There were also words such as 'left' and 'right', which described the position of the objects with respect to the dolphin, and enabled it to identify a specific object, e.g. left hoop versus right hoop. The vocabulary of some 30 to 40 words, together with word-order rules, allowed for many thousands of unique sentences to be constructed, the simplest being instructions to the dolphin to perform named actions to named objects. In one experiment conducted by Herman's team, a sequence of two gestures, which roughly meant 'surfboard over', directed the dolphin to leap over the surfboard. More complex sentences required the dolphin to construct a relationship between two objects, such as taking one named object to another named object. To interpret the relational sentences correctly, the dolphin had to take account of both word meaning and word order.

evidence.quote: During the 1960s, researchers attempted to understand whether the whistle vocalizations might be a form of language. Investigators recorded whistles from many dolphins in many different situations, but soon realized the vocalizations were not complicated enough to support anything approaching a human language system. Some of the early work instead pointed to the stereotype of the whistles from individual dolphins, which led researchers David and Melba Caldwell to suggest that the whistle functioned principally as a 'signature', with each individual dolphin producing a distinctive signature. Presumably, this enabled that individual to be identified by others.

evidence.quote: Dolphins have been tested in many formal procedures, leading to a fuller understanding of their competencies. In general, high levels of parental care and high degrees of brain activity go together. It is easy to see how the extensive development of the brain in dolphins, and the resulting cognitive skills of some members of this group, have derived from the demands of survival in the dolphin community. These challenges include both co- operation and competition among peers, particularly important because of the prolonged development of the young.

evidence.quote: Dolphins produce various types of sounds, including clicks, burst- pulse emissions, and whistles. Clicks are used for echolocation – the dolphin's form of sonar – which allows the dolphin to examine its world by listening to the echoes returning from objects struck by the clicks. Sounds such as whistling may indicate the dolphin's psychological state, ranging from pleasure to anger. However, much remains to be learned about these types of vocalizations. For example, it is unclear whether these whistles are intentionally used for communication.

evidence.quote: From the mid-1950s to the mid-1960s, researcher John Lilly promoted the idea that bottlenose dolphins might possess an innate language. He based his supposition on this species' exceptionally large brain. He reasoned that this must be a powerful information processor having capabilities for advanced levels of intellectual accomplishment, including the development of a language. He set about to uncover the supposed language. Failing in that quest, he then attempted, also ineffectively, to get the dolphins which he kept in his laboratories to understand human vocal language – English in this case.

evidence.quote: No single trait has been linked more closely with the human species than language. However, the definition of language and its uniqueness as a human trait continue to be studied and debated. Some scholars, such as the linguist Noam Chomsky, take the view that language is an adaptation supported by specialist modifications of the brain that appear only in humans. Others, such as the anthropologist Barbara King, favor a continuity position, which suggests that language must have its roots in early human forms of communication, and that some of these may still exist in modern animal species.

evidence.quote: The Kewalo Basin dolphin language studies of the mid-1970s, which were begun by Louis Herman and colleagues, emphasized language comprehension from the start. The researchers, working principally with a bottlenose dolphin named Akeakamai, constructed a sign language in which the gestures of a person's arms and hands corresponded to words. The words referred to objects from Akeakamai's habitat, and what the dolphin could do with them. There were also words such as 'left' and 'right', which described the position of the objects with respect to the dolphin, and enabled it to identify a specific object, e.g. left hoop versus right hoop. The vocabulary of some 30 to 40 words, together with word-order rules, allowed for many thousands of unique sentences to be constructed, the simplest being instructions to the dolphin to perform named actions to named objects. In one experiment conducted by Herman's team, a sequence of two gestures, which roughly meant 'surfboard over', directed the dolphin to leap over the surfboard. More complex sentences required the dolphin to construct a relationship between two objects, such as taking one named object to another named object. To interpret the relational sentences correctly, the dolphin had to take account of both word meaning and word order.

evidence.quote: In the primitive insect societies, conflict and competition lead to the emergence of a single female, the queen, which physically dominates the rest of the adult members of the colony. In the more advanced insect societies, particularly those in which strong differences between the queen and worker castes exist, the queen also exercises control over the workers, but usually in a more subtle manner, without obvious aggression. This evolutionary change, from what might be regarded as rough dominance to the more refined methods of queen control, is one of the clear-cut adaptations that extend across the social insects as a whole, and one worth tracing in some detail.

14.explanation: Tiến hóa từ áp đảo thô sang kiểm soát tinh tế là xu hướng nhất quán.

evidence.quote: Aggression and dominance were first recorded by the Swiss scientist Pierre Huber (1802) In his pioneering study of bumblebees. He saw that when a queen lays her eggs, some of the workers try to steal and eat them, but the queen usually repels these Intruders with great anger. Similar findings have been reported by a long line of subsequent investigators. The Austrian Eduard Hoffer (1882-1883) discovered that: 'punishment is almost always administered with the legs and mandibles, and the guilty individual never even attempts to defend herself, all her efforts being directed toward making the quickest possible escape. The punishment is sometimes so rough that the poor creature is seriously wounded or even killed.' Once egg stealing has been repelled for a few hours, the attempts by the workers become less and less frequent, and finally cease altogether; and these same little Insects which previously tried 'their very best to get rid of the newly-laid eggs, now become attentive guardians and nurses of their embryo brothers and sisters; they keep them warm and tenderly provide them with nourishment continuously thereafter.'

15.explanation: Huber và Hoffer ghi những quan sát sớm về hung hăng.

evidence.quote: Egg stealing puzzled the early observers; it seemed to them such strange behaviour, as if the bumblebees were heading for race suicide. Huber offered a surprisingly modern hypothesis. He stated: ‘The bumblebees are the largest insects that feed on honey; and if their number trebled or quadrupled, other insects would not find any nourishment, and perhaps their species would be wiped out.' Perez (1899) viewed egg eating as simply evidence of selfish behaviour on the part of the workers, and therefore an Imperfection in the social order. But there is a more straightforward explanation of the phenomenon: Lindhard (1912) observed an Instance In which a queen of the species Bombus lapidaries extracted the egg of a rival worker and fed it to a queen larva. Also noting that very few, if any, worker-laid eggs ever survive, he hypothesized that the objects are not meant to develop but instead provide food for prospective queens. If there is any truth in this conclusion, It Is consistent with the general occurrence of unfertilized eggs laid by workers of related insect species.

16.explanation: Nhiều giả thuyết giải thích hành vi ăn trứng tưởng tự hủy.

evidence.quote: The existence of a similar dominance system in the paper wasp, Polistes gallicus, was suggested by Heldmann (1936), who found that when two or more females start a nest together, one comes to function as the main egg layer, and therefore queen, while the others take up the role of workers. The queen feeds more on the eggs laid by the workers than the reverse, thus exercising a form of reproductive dominance. However, the relationship among the adult members of the wasp colony is somewhat more elaborate in form than that in bumblebee colonies. Instead of simple dictatorship by the queen, there exists in most cases a series of ranks, involving a principal egg layer, the queen, and the remainder of the associated females, called auxiliaries. The relative intensities of egg laying, food gathering, and comb building are graded accordingly. Dominant individuals receive more food whenever food is exchanged, they lay more eggs, and they contribute less work. They establish and maintain their rank by a series of frequently repeated aggressive encounters.

17.explanation: Xếp hạng gắn với được ăn nhiều, đẻ nhiều và làm ít.

evidence.quote: At their lowest intensity these encounters are simply a matter of posture; the dominant individual rises on its legs to a level higher than the subordinate, while the subordinate crouches and lowers its antennae. At higher intensities leg biting occurs, and at highest intensity the wasps attempt to sting each other. The severest conflicts occur between wasps of nearly equal rank, and during the early days of the association when the nest is first being constructed. As time passes, the wasps fit more easily into their roles, and aggressive exchanges become more subdued, less frequent, and eventually purely postural in nature. When the first adult workers emerge from the pupa*, during later stages of colony development, their relations to the founders of the colony are invariably subordinate and non-violent. The workers also form a hierarchy among themselves; those that emerge early tend to dominate their younger nestmates. If the head female is removed, the next highest auxiliaries intensify their hostility to each other until one of their number becomes definitely dominant; then the exchanges subside to the previous low level.

18.explanation: Tư thế, cắn chân và đốt là các mức hung hăng.

evidence.quote: Eberhard (1969) found that the tropical wasp species Polistes canadensis differs from species found in temperate regions of the world, in that its contests are more violent and result in the losers leaving the nest. The queens are also less dependent on the indirect technique of egg eating to maintain reproductive control. Thus Polistes canadensis approaches a condition of true dictatorship, whereas all the temperate species that have been studied up till now possess a colony organization that can be characterized as an uneasy oligarchy**.

evidence.quote: Throughout history, clothing has served many social purposes. One of the most fundamental aspects of dress in most societies is the custom that the dress of men and women should be different. These differences reflect culturally-determined views of the social roles appropriate to each gender. What is considered appropriate may differ markedly from one place to another. For many centuries in Western Europe, for example, trousers were generally designated as male dress. Clothing may also serve to mark age associated changes. Thus throughout the 19th century, younger girls in Western Europe wore shorter skirts than their adolescent sisters. What a person wears may also convey other information about the wearer, as when a wedding ring worn on a specific finger signifies that he or she is in a marital relationship. Similarly, it was once customary in Europe for married women to cover their hair, while young unmarried women were permitted to go without head covering.

evidence.quote: Dress, therefore, discloses the social stratification of society, revealing whether it has rigid delineations of social and economic class or is a relatively classless society. For example, the political leaders in the African Ashanti tribe wore distinctive dress marking their special social position. No subject was allowed to wear the same fabric pattern as the king. The nature of this political structure — an absolute monarchy — was mirrored in the attitude to clothing. Other aspects of social organization may be manifest in dress. The garments worn by those leading a religious service may or may not distinguish them from the worshippers, again reflecting the way that religion is seen by members of that community.

3.explanation: Lễ phục phản ánh cách cộng đồng nhìn tôn giáo.

evidence.quote: As well as differentiating between social groups, clothing also serves other purposes. Sociologists speak of rites of passage, marking the passage of the individual from one status to another. Specific costumes exist in modern American society that are considered appropriate for graduations, weddings, baptisms, and burials. Special clothing may also be involved in ceremonies which serve to strengthen the community, as when the inhabitants of a town dress in historic costume to celebrate the anniversary of the founding of the town. Designated forms of dress are frequently an important part of the ceremonies associated with such rites. Clothing is also a means of enhancing the attractiveness of individuals. This may be achieved by focusing attention on a particular part of the body, or by clothes which make the wearer appear affluent and successful.

evidence.quote: The production of textiles and clothing is closely related to the advance of technology. One dramatic example from the 19th and early 20th centuries was the increase in the mass production of clothing in the United States, which made possible the modern fashion industry. Technology may also have an impact on areas such as transportation, communications or production of consumer goods, each of which in turn may affect dress. Examples range from the invention of the sewing machine, without which mass production would have been impossible, to the development of the bicycle, which encouraged the wearing of shorter skirts by women.

evidence.quote: In some cultures, certain types of clothing have been restricted to persons of a particular social rank. These restrictions were sometimes codified into what were known as 'Sumptuary Laws', which restricted the use of luxury goods such as clothing and household furnishings. Thus during the 14th century in England servants were not permitted to wear any article of gold or silver, embroidery or silver. Nowadays, dress is still used to identify an individual as belonging to a particular social group. A uniform or insignia may be adopted formally by that group and kept for its members alone. At other times, group identification is demonstrated by an informal kind of uniform, such as those adopted by adolescents who belong to the same clique.

Fashion may be affected when governments pass legislation to regulate clothing-related industries, or by the desire of individuals or groups to imitate clothing worn by charismatic political leaders. evidence.quote: One of the biggest ranches was owned by the Aztec Land and Cattle Company, which owned a million acres of land by 1884. Each acre had cost the company a mere 50 cents, and like many other speculators, it was only interested in quick profits and had little incentive to protect the soils from overgrazing. By the time Aztec sold the ranch in 1901, it was barren, with cattle carcasses scattered across the exhausted land. Such was the damage to the grasslands that even now few of the pastures have recovered. The parched and exposed soil simply blew away. The 1862 Homestead Act was passed in order to encourage the populating of the West. Any family willing to make the journey was entitled to claim 160 acres and farm it. The water sources were therefore cut off, and were aggressively guarded. It was only in the 1930s, with the passage of the Taylor Grazing Act, that federal authorities finally sought to limit cattle herds.

They carry nutrients with them into areas which previously evolved and survived without them. But perhaps the most dramatic impact of the dust has been on snowfields in the Rocky Mountain Range.
